n: Ezekiel is told to sing a funeral lament (a qinah) for Israel’s “princes”—the last kings of Judah. It is written in the limping rhythm of Hebrew funeral songs.

f.g: Hebrew qinah, a dirge with a distinctive 3+2 beat rhythm.
Ezekiel’s usual term for Judah’s kings.

n: The “mother” is Judah (or the royal house), pictured as a lioness raising cubs among lions. The lion was Judah’s ancient emblem.
One cub grows into a young lion that learns to hunt and devours people—King Jehoahaz, who reigned only three months and did evil.
The nations trapped him and dragged him in hooks to Egypt. Pharaoh Necho deposed Jehoahaz and took him to Egypt, where he died.

f.w: they brought him with chains unto the land of Egypt
f.g: Literally “with hooks,” as captured animals were led.

n: When her hope was gone, the lioness raised another cub to be a young lion—most likely Jehoiachin (or possibly Zedekiah).

f.g: Probably Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC; some suggest Zedekiah.

n: He prowled among the lions, learned to hunt, and devoured people—another king who ruled by violence rather than justice.
He destroyed strongholds and ravaged cities; the land was terrified by his roaring.

f.g: The Hebrew is difficult; probably “he ravaged their strongholds.”

n: The surrounding nations set a net and caught him in their pit.
Caged and chained, he was brought to the king of Babylon so his roar would no longer be heard on Israel’s mountains.

f.w: brought him to the king of Babylon

n: The image changes: the mother is now a vine planted by plentiful water, fruitful and full of branches—Judah in its prosperous days.

f.w: like a vine in thy blood
f.g: The Hebrew is unclear; perhaps “a vine in your vineyard.”

n: Her strong branches became royal scepters, and she stood tall among the clouds—the Davidic dynasty at its height.

f.w: strong rods for the sceptres of them that bare rule

n: But she was ripped up in anger and thrown down. The east wind dried her fruit, and fire burned her strongest branches.

f.w: the east wind dried up her fruit

n: Now she is replanted in a dry, thirsty desert—Judah in exile in Babylon.
Fire spread from one of her own branches—Zedekiah’s rebellion—and consumed her, leaving no strong branch to rule. “This is a lament, and has become a lament”: the prophecy was turning into history.

f.w: fire is gone out of a rod of her branches
f.g: The destruction came from within the royal family itself.

f.w: she hath no strong rod to be a sceptre to rule
